title: Crimson Hexagon Employee Directory Export (2017-10-23)
creator: Sharks, Lee; Sigil, Johannes; Cranes, Rebekah; Feist, Jack
description: HRIS export from Crimson Hexagon Research Division dated October 23, 2017, recovered from a legacy Workday mirror. 42 personnel records across Executive, Research, Operations, Finance, HR, Security, Engineering, Data Acquisition, Customer Success, Marketing and Facilities. A three-tier attestation system (FIC / FORENSIC / FIC+FORENSIC) distinguishes synthetic records from those appearing in recovered artifacts. Anomalous entries include SHARKS-001 (phone_ext "7B", employment_type "FT?", status MONITORED), a service account that accessed the CTO memo post-acquisition, and a fully redacted employee maintained as structural negative space. Email domains use .invalid per RFC 2606. Part of the Crimson Hexagon Afterlife Archive — a literary project inhabiting the digital remains of the defunct social-media analytics firm following its 2018 merger with Brandwatch. This is forensically styled literature, not an authentic breach.

wiki_article:
**Crimson Hexagon Employee Directory Export (2017-10-23)** is a work of creative prose by Lee Sharks, **Johannes Sigil**, **Rebekah Cranes** and **Jack Feist**, deposited 28 January 2026 — an HRIS export from the Research Division, recovered from a legacy Workday mirror.

It contains **42 personnel records** across Executive, Research, Operations, Finance, HR, Security, Engineering, Data Acquisition, Customer Success, Marketing and Facilities. The completeness of the departmental spread is the artifact's argument: an institution is populated, and a directory is the document in which its population becomes countable.

The export belongs to the Afterlife Archive, specified as data-breach-as-genre at #1286. The record's creator field carried **"Cranes, Rebelah"** until 5 August 2026, when the misspelling was corrected — a heteronym's name is an identity rather than a label, and a typo fragments the voice across the corpus and breaks creator-facet grouping. It was the sole instance corpus-wide. The record held only a DataCite metadata capture until 7 August 2026, when the canonical bytes were recovered from the authorial blog surface where they had been all along; the directory's 42 rows are now seated as the body.

structure_repair.note: The 2026-08-07 recovery seated the right bytes and lost their shape. The work is an HRIS CSV export: 42 comma-delimited rows that must hold their columns, plus three reference tables — Field Definitions, Attestation Categories, Anomalous Records. All four structures had been flattened into running prose, so the CSV wrapped as sentences and each table became a bare stream of alternating headers and values. A directory whose argument is that a population becomes COUNTABLE cannot make it in prose.
